name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
facts: A communist leader detained under the Preventive Detention Act challenged his detention.
held: The Court read Articles 19, 21 and 22 as separate compartments and gave 'procedure established by law' a narrow meaning: any procedure enacted by law was enough.
why: The starting point that Maneka Gandhi later overturned. Useful for showing how Article 21 evolved.

name: I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab
facts: Land-owning families challenged land reform laws placed beyond judicial review by constitutional amendments.
held: Parliament could not amend the Constitution to take away or abridge Fundamental Rights.
why: Triggered the 24th Amendment and set the stage for Kesavananda Bharati.

name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
facts: A religious head challenged Kerala land reform laws and the constitutional amendments protecting them. A 13-judge bench heard the case.
held: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but cannot alter its basic structure, such as supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review and federalism.
why: The basic structure doctrine: the single most important constitutional case in India.

name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
facts: Challenge to the 39th Amendment, which placed the Prime Minister's election beyond judicial scrutiny.
held: The amendment clause protecting the election was struck down for violating free and fair elections, part of the basic structure.
why: First application of the basic structure doctrine to strike down an amendment.

name: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla
facts: During the Emergency, detenues filed habeas corpus petitions after enforcement of Article 21 was suspended.
held: The majority held that no one could approach courts for enforcement of Article 21 during the Emergency. Justice H.R. Khanna dissented.
why: Expressly overruled in Puttaswamy (2017). Khanna J's dissent is a classic on liberty.

name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
facts: The petitioner's passport was impounded without giving reasons or a hearing.
held: Any procedure depriving life or liberty must be fair, just and reasonable, not arbitrary. Articles 14, 19 and 21 are interlinked (the 'golden triangle').
why: Transformed Article 21 into a source of many rights through due process.

name: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar
facts: Newspaper reports revealed thousands of undertrials in Bihar jails for longer than the maximum sentence for their offences.
held: Speedy trial is part of Article 21, and the State must provide free legal aid to the poor accused.
why: Foundation of speedy trial and legal aid jurisprudence; led to the release of thousands of undertrials.

name: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
facts: Challenge to the 42nd Amendment clauses giving Parliament unlimited amending power and placing Directive Principles above Fundamental Rights.
held: Limited amending power and the harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are part of the basic structure.
why: Reaffirmed Kesavananda and protected judicial review.

name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
facts: Pavement dwellers in Bombay challenged their eviction without notice.
held: The right to livelihood is part of the right to life. Evictions must follow a fair procedure with notice.
why: Expanded Article 21 to include livelihood.

name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum gas leak)
facts: Oleum gas leaked from a Shriram plant in Delhi, harming residents.
held: Enterprises engaged in hazardous activities are absolutely liable for harm, without the exceptions available under strict liability.
why: Created the Indian rule of absolute liability.

name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
facts: Challenge to 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes in central government jobs (Mandal Commission).
held: OBC reservation upheld, the creamy layer must be excluded, and total reservation should ordinarily not exceed 50%.
why: The leading case on reservations and the 50% ceiling.

name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
facts: Challenge to the dismissal of State governments under President's Rule.
held: Proclamations under Article 356 are subject to judicial review; majority must be tested on the floor of the House. Secularism is part of the basic structure.
why: Curbed misuse of President's Rule and protected federalism.

name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
facts: A letter to the Chief Justice highlighted deaths in police custody.
held: Laid down mandatory arrest guidelines: identification of officers, arrest memo, informing a relative, medical examination, and access to a lawyer.
why: Its guidelines are now written into BNSS Sections 36, 38 and 48.

name: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
facts: Following the gang rape of a social worker in Rajasthan, women's groups sought protection against sexual harassment at work.
held: Issued binding guidelines on preventing sexual harassment at the workplace, relying on international conventions until Parliament legislated.
why: Led to the POSH Act, 2013.

name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
facts: Police failed to register an FIR about a missing minor girl.
held: Registration of an FIR is mandatory when information discloses a cognizable offence; a preliminary inquiry is allowed only in limited categories.
why: Key FIR case. BNSS Section 173 now allows a preliminary enquiry for offences punishable from 3 to 7 years.

name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
facts: Concern over routine arrests in dowry harassment cases under Section 498A IPC.
held: Police must not arrest automatically for offences punishable up to seven years; they must record reasons and follow the checklist, and magistrates must check before authorising detention.
why: Applies now to BNSS Section 35 and BNS Section 85.

name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
facts: Arrests over social media posts under Section 66A of the IT Act.
held: Section 66A was struck down as vague and overbroad, violating free speech.
why: Landmark on online speech and the test of vagueness.

name: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
facts: A woman challenged instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat).
held: Instant triple talaq was set aside by a 3:2 majority as arbitrary and unconstitutional.
why: Led to the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.

name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
facts: Aadhaar-related challenges raised whether privacy is a Fundamental Right. A 9-judge bench heard the question.
held: Privacy is a Fundamental Right intrinsic to Article 21 and Part III. ADM Jabalpur was overruled.
why: The foundation of Indian data protection law.

name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
facts: Challenge to Section 377 IPC as it criminalised consensual same-sex relations.
held: Section 377 was read down to decriminalise consensual sexual acts between adults.
why: Major ruling on dignity, equality and sexual orientation.

name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
facts: Challenge to adultery as a crime under Section 497 IPC, which treated the wife as the husband's property.
held: Section 497 was struck down as arbitrary and discriminatory.
why: Adultery is no longer a crime; it may still be a ground for divorce.

name: Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose
facts: A minor mortgaged his property to a moneylender, who later sought to enforce it.
held: An agreement with a minor is void from the beginning, and the minor cannot be made to return the money received.
why: The leading case under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act.
